title: Stop Climbing, Start Cultivating: Aimee Rickabus on Women's Later Seasons
guestBio: Pam Roy is a writer, investor, and philanthropist who co-founded the Viktor E. Frankl Institute of America and B-Unbound. She is the author of Parenting from the Passenger Seat, co-author of Viktor E. Frankl and the Search for Meaning (Beacon Press, 2025), and an executive producer of The Friendship Bench documentary. Her forthcoming book, The Education Pivot: Meaning and Mattering in the Age of AI, co-authored with Elliot Washor, is due from Beacon Press in January 2027.
excerpt: Aimee Rickabus hands the mic to author and Viktor Frankl Institute co-founder Pam Roy — and for the first time, Aimee is the one answering the questions. Together they explore why the ladder was never the whole story, what the four seasons of a woman's life really mean, and how the wound becomes the soil for everything that grows next.
metaDescription: Aimee Rickabus & Pam Roy explore the four seasons of a woman's life, the garden vs. ladder metaphor, and what it means to cultivate rather than climb.
keyTakeaways: The ladder is a culturally inherited model of success that can quietly become an excuse to avoid inner work and the deeper life you've been putting off.
Life reimagined as a garden — with seasons of planting, blooming, harvest, and rest — gives women permission to grow in ways that climbing never could.
Motherhood is not a woman's highest contribution; it may be her greatest apprenticeship, preparing her with empathy, wisdom, and emotional intelligence for the seasons that follow.
Viktor Frankl's insight that meaning is always available — and that we need many meanings, not one singular purpose — is a lifeline during every season of transition.
The worthiness wound — the deeply held belief that you are not enough — often drives high-achieving women to climb harder rather than look inward, and healing it changes everything.
Cultivating a life is not a luxury reserved for the privileged; it begins with one honest conversation about where you need help, and with building the community willing to share the load.
When women in their fall and winter seasons claim their wisdom and stop competing, the ripple effect reaches not just their own families but the generations on both sides of the timeline.

pullQuotes.text: I was going to the top and I was climbing, climbing, climbing — and in some ways I feel like I was running away from the pain, from the wounds, from childhood wounds.
The ladder in a lot of ways will be an excuse to avoid doing the inner work, to avoid even doing the someday things that you've always wanted to do.
This may be the greatest misunderstanding about women. We assume motherhood is our highest contribution. Perhaps motherhood is our apprenticeship.
Soil can be restored. It can be aerated, replenished, watered, and brought back to its full potential. The same is true of you.
Women, you are allowed to go do all the things that men get to do. The fine print was you still have to do all of the things that women do too — because men aren't going to do them.

quiz.title: Which Season of Your Garden Are You Cultivating Right Now?
quiz.description: This isn't a test — there are no wrong answers here. These six questions will help you discover which season of your inner garden is most alive right now, and what kind of cultivation your soul is quietly asking for.

A.name: The Spring Planter
A.description: You are in a season of bold beginnings and brave firsts. You're learning who you are on your own terms, planting seeds you can't yet see the harvest of, and discovering that your ambition and your authenticity don't have to be in conflict. The world may be telling you to climb faster — but something deeper is calling you to root down first. This episode will give you the language and permission to honor both the drive and the longing at the same time.

B.name: The Summer Builder
B.description: You are in the full heat of building — your career, your family, your reputation, and possibly all three at once. You are capable of extraordinary things, and you are also quietly exhausted by the second shift nobody talks about. This episode will name what you've been carrying without a word for it, and remind you that the ladder was never meant to be your whole story — even now, in your most productive season.

C.name: The Fall Harvester
C.description: You are stepping into one of the most underrated seasons of a woman's life — a time of transition, recalibration, and the kind of wisdom that only comes from having actually lived. You may be mourning something that has ended, while something new and unexpected is quietly asking for your attention. This episode was practically written for you, and Aimee's words about the fall garden will feel like someone finally said out loud what you've been feeling alone.

D.name: The Winter Cultivator
D.description: You have lived enough seasons to know that winter is not the end — it is the deep, essential rest that makes spring possible. You carry a kind of wisdom that your culture does not fully celebrate yet, and you are learning to offer it on your own terms. This episode will remind you that the grandmothers on the Friendship Bench, the elder orcas leading migration, and the women in their winter seasons have always been the ones who hold humanity together — and that includes you.

questions.question: When you think about the life you're living right now, what's the feeling that shows up most honestly?

options.text: Anticipation — I'm just getting started and there's so much ahead of me.
Momentum — I'm deep in it, building hard, and I don't want to slow down.
Transition — something significant has shifted or ended, and I'm still finding my footing.
Reflection — I'm looking back as much as forward, and finding meaning in both directions.

questions.question: When you imagine "the someday things" — the life you've been putting off — what does that feel like?

options.text: Exciting and a little scary — they still feel possible if I move now.
Frustrating — I know what I want but I genuinely don't have the time or space yet.
Urgent — I've been waiting long enough and I can feel the clock ticking.
Peaceful — I've started doing some of them, and it feels like coming home.

questions.question: If you're honest with yourself, what does your relationship with achievement feel like right now?

options.text: I'm still building my definition of success — I want to get it right from the start.
I'm driven and proud of what I've built, but I sometimes wonder what I've traded for it.
I'm questioning the ladder itself — I climbed it and I'm not sure it led where I thought.
I've made peace with achievement — it was one season, not the whole story.

questions.question: How do you relate to asking for help?

options.text: I'm learning how — I know I need it but I'm still figuring out how to ask without feeling like I'm failing.
It's hard. I'm usually the one people come to, and asking feels like losing ground.
I'm getting better at it — I've started to see it as wisdom rather than weakness.
It feels natural now — I've seen enough to know none of us were meant to do this alone.

questions.question: When you think about your most meaningful contribution to the world, what comes up?

options.text: I'm still discovering it — I want to build something that truly matters.
It's the work I do and the people I'm raising — but sometimes they feel like they're competing for me.
It's starting to shift — the roles that defined me are changing and I'm finding new ones.
It lives in what I model, mentor, and pass on — the harvest from every season before this one.

questions.question: What does the idea of "tending to your own soil" bring up for you?

options.text: Curiosity — I'm just beginning to understand what that even means for me.
Guilt — I know I need to do it, but everyone else's needs seem to come first.
Relief — I've started doing some of this work and it's hard, but it's real.
Gratitude — the inner work has been the most important garden I've ever tended.

transcript: I was going to the top and I was climbing, climbing, climbing, and in some ways I feel like I was running away from the pain, from the wounds, from childhood wounds, from even the the wounds that my parents had carried as children. You know, are we climbing this ladder to get away from all the pain? Do we think we can buy our way out of dealing with our own stuff? I had kind of [music] put off doing my life five years at a time because there was always this other thing that I had to do. There was this other rung that I had to climb. You know, I had to keep going, keep going. I was always very success driven. I always wanted to get to the next revenue marker for the companies, you know, get that next big account, go chase it. [music] And thinking that once you get this, you can do that. So the ladder in a lot of ways will be an excuse [music] to avoid doing the inner work, to avoid even doing the someday things that you've always wanted to do. Women, [music] you are allowed to go do all the things that men get to do. The fine print was you still have to do all of the things that women do too [music] because men aren't going to do them. >> [music] >> Welcome to the Man Age Her, the podcast where we explore the extraordinary lives of women and the invisible work they do and the ways we're redefining what it means to lead, live, and thrive. I'm your host, Amy Rickabaugh, entrepreneur, author, and mother of six. Today we're doing something a little different. For the first time I'm turning the microphone around and letting someone else ask the questions and there's a very special reason for that. This Friday, November 20th, my second book, The Cultivate Her, When Women Stop Climbing and Start Cultivating, officially launches. And I have to tell you, this book has been a journey. When I wrote my first book, The Man Age Her, I wanted to shine a light on the invisible work women do, the work of raising families, managing households, building relationships, and holding so many things together often go unrecognized. I wanted women to understand that this work develops extraordinary leadership capabilities. But as I continue to exploring women's lives, I found myself asking a different question. What if we've been measuring success against the wrong standard? We've been taught that life is a ladder, that success means climbing higher, achieving more, pushing harder, and constantly striving for the next thing. But the more I looked at my own life, the more I began to wonder whether that model really reflected the way women live, grow, and contribute. What if life isn't a ladder at all? What if life is a garden? What if instead of constantly asking ourselves what we need to achieve next, we began asking what we want to cultivate? The question became the foundation of the Cultivate Her. And today, I've invited someone very special to help me explore it. Pam Roy is an author, co-founder of the Viktor Frankl Institute of America, and someone I've come to know as a dear friend and collaborator. Pam also wrote the foreword to The Cultivate Her. She brings such a thoughtful perspective to conversations about meaning, purpose, and the different seasons of our lives. And because she's been a part of this journey, I thought she would be the perfect person to turn the tables on me. So today, Pam is taking over the interview. We're going to talk about the personal journey behind the book, the ideas that shaped it, and what might become possible when women began looking at their lives through a different lens. The question we're managing today is, what if success isn't about how high we climb, but about what we cultivate along the way? Pam, welcome back to The Manage Her, and thank you for agreeing to put me in the hot seat today. I am so excited. >> I am so excited, and I am so grateful to be back here with you. I love our conversations. So I've had the privilege of reading The Cultivate Her, and was very honored that you asked me to write the foreword. What struck me most is that this book is about much more than redefining success. It's about how we as women understand ourselves, our purpose, and the contributions we make throughout our lives. I'd love to explore some questions with you that get at the heart of the book. First, I want to talk about your personal journey because you have shared with me how this book actually unfolded some ongoing revelations for you as you wrote the book. So you spent decades raising children, building businesses, and creating opportunities for others. What began to change for you? Was there a moment when you realized that the definition of success you had been pursuing was no longer the whole story? And how did the journey of writing the Manage Her ultimately lead you to this book? >> Oh man, it's so interesting. I think the Manage Her and writing the Manage Her was kind of this naming the wound kind of part of my journey. It was sort of naming all of this hard work that I'd been doing in the background unnoticed and kind of without getting the applause, the recognition, the monetary, you know, benefits that you get for regular work. All of a sudden it was like it was a way for me to name that, to own it, and to re-empower my own self. Like yes, you are doing all this work. It is important. It is highly skilled. I needed that for myself. I think when you come up against imposter syndrome and you feel like you're not enough or you haven't done enough. If you start naming all the things you have done, it's kind of the cure for that. I had a coach and she asked me to write 100 things that I had done in my life that I was proud of. And it's one of the most amazing exercises you can do for yourself, actually. And so writing that book was the first step. And then after I finished that book, it wasn't really it wasn't over for me. I started thinking about human potential and I really thought the next thing I was going to write was going to be a curriculum on human potential for high school aged children. That was what I was going to write. That's where I started out, and this is where I ended up. And that that's sort of the writing journey, I think, as a writer. I think as your life unfolds in these kinds of books, especially my own personal experiences as I'm writing the book, a lot of times they're unfolding as I'm writing. It's like a real life experience. The things that I was going through as I was beginning the journey of writing this book unveiled a whole another layer to me. You know, I ended up going through a real personal journey of dealing with some of my own wounds and really traveling inward into my own soil and discovering that this this ladder that I'd been climbing I was going to the top and I was climbing, climbing, climbing and in some ways I feel like I was running away from the pain, from the wounds, from childhood wounds, from even the the wounds that my parents had carried as children. You know, are we climbing this ladder to get away from all the pain? Do we think we can buy our way out of dealing with our own stuff? And I think we do live in a society that's been sold that. I decided to climb down the ladder and get dirty and get my hands dirty and start really trying to figure out what was motivating the behavior, how could I start seeing myself in a clearer way, more clarity kind of getting into the shadows of myself. And that's what this book really was. This book was for me my personal shift from climbing the ladder and then climbing down into my garden and starting to cultivate my own self. >> That's wonderful. And so much of what you say and write about in the book is relatable to so many women. I found myself nodding and recognizing my my own self in your stories and and appreciate so much the vulnerability that you brought to telling the story. So your central metaphor is that life is a garden, not a ladder, which is a very powerful way of looking at life. It's simple, but it challenges so much of what our culture teaches us about achievement. What does it mean to cultivate a life rather than climb through one? And does that mean giving up ambition or redefining it? >> Woo. Yeah. It was climb, climb, climb for me. And having only the model of the ladder, like for my whole lifetime, what I realized, you know, was that I had kind of put off doing my life five years at a time because there was always this other thing that I had to do. There was this other rung that I had to climb. You know, I had to keep going, keep going. It was all about for me it had really always been I was always very success driven. I always wanted to get to the next revenue marker for the companies, you know, get that next big account, go chase it and thinking that once you get this, you can do that. So there's this someday aspect of life and when you start really putting off all the things you really, really want to do. And so the ladder in a lot of ways will be an excuse to avoid doing the inner work, to avoid even doing the someday things that you've always wanted to do. I love Jen Drummond talking about somedays. We had her on the show the beginning of this month with Extraordinary Women and her whole thing is about someday right now. And I realized when I talk about this book, there's a passage that I'd love to read. This is from page 43. For most of my life I was climbing, chasing goals, titles, numbers, and milestones, trying to get somewhere higher, faster, better, living my life off five years at a time since I was 17 years old. But no matter how high I climbed, there was always another rung, another goal, another pressure to keep going. Just another five years and then all. And one day I was working on this book about humanity and human potential and it hit me, the garden. A garden doesn't climb aimlessly to the sky. It grows. It roots down deep before it reaches up. It needs seasons of stillness, seasons of rest, seasons of blooming, and seasons of fruit. And really finding that shift in myself, climbing down that ladder and realizing that I have all of these beds in my garden that need tending. I have this soil that needs to be tended and amended and there's so much to having this fertile soil in our life, which is as my mother would really call it like emotional groceries. Like have you dealt with your wounds? You know, is there anything festering inside of you that you need to deal with? Some emotional wound that you've just been avoiding? And this is the work that I've really being I'm being called into. I'm working with a client right now and as he's addressing his wounds, he's able, you know, as instead of running from his wounds, he's actually addressing them. He's looking at them. He's taking time to feel those things. And in the feeling and the honoring of the wound, it's like once you allow yourself to feel the pain, you can move through it and you can heal from it. But avoiding it doesn't heal it at all. >> Well, I think also the other point to that is that in a garden for plants to flourish, they don't flourish alone, just like regenerative farming. You need to have the bees to pollinate and you need to have the different fungi and you need to have the different kind of plants that do it. So this goes to how you and I originally connected was recognizing how important it is that we support each other in being able to to do this and to look at ourselves and knowing that we are part of a greater whole and that each of us is a very, very critical part plays a critical role in the flourishing of any garden. So I love that. And so that leads to the next question, which really relates to the seasons that you just introduced. And I love this metaphor, the seasons of of a woman's life. So you describe the seasons as the seasons of spring, summer, fall, and winter, each with its own gifts and possibilities. Why is it so important that we recognize and honor these seasons rather than expecting women to remain forever in a season of producing, achieving, and caring for others, which we have for generations taken on. And I think it's it's come at quite a price to our health and well-being as we've continued to try to nurture this society that ever increasingly becomes mechanistic and faster and external. And hello. Where do we go from here? >> So as we begin to recognize our seasons, we can honor them, right? I mean, what I realized is that we live in a culture that is all about spring and summer. We celebrate youth and fertility, and we expect women to stay in the spring and summer for as long as absolutely possible, and then they become invisible. And it is brutal. I mean, we live in Southern California where beauty is a commodity. Beauty is commoditized. It is commercialized. It is a billion dollar industry, you know, from everything from Botox to fillers to facelifts to threads to you name it, lasers and all of the things. Youth is sold on a daily basis to women over the age of 40. And nowadays, I feel like they're pushing it on women who are even younger. And I would love to see our society make a shift where we start understanding that spring and summer are fabulous, yes. But motherhood is actually the apprenticeship for something much more important for humanity, which is this time of fall and winter, which is in mammals and humans in general, very, very rare that you see species that have postmenopausal females. So we see it in elephants. We see it in orca whales. These societies are matriarchal. These societies have these women in their groups for a reason. These women carry the memories, the females, these older female elephants know where the water is when there's a drought. They know where the deep water is. These female orcas lead migration patterns. We are the cultivators. We are the what is missing in the world is connected women in their fall and winter seasons who understand intuition, have healed their wounds, and are ready to do the work of cultivating themselves, each other, and the rest of humanity. We're the people. We are the ones. We're the ones who will lead humanity through. We are the ones who will help to bring through the next generation that we can bring together this wisdom and knowledge of this lifetime that we've spent, all of the things we've learned as younger women, all of the things we've learned as mothers, the empathy, the emotional IQ, all of the things that you learn, how to manage [snorts] vast amounts of information at one time, and managing education for these children, and all the things we do as mothers. You know, I think that we've just simply overlooked the idea. I think that our culture simply has missed that this is an also a very important part of humanity, that these older females are We are the old wise women. We are not to be discarded. And I love what you did with your documentary with Dixon Chibanda. And I would I mean, tell the girls about this documentary because it is just This is what I'm talking about. >> Yes. So it's called The Friendship Bench. And there was a psychiatrist in Zimbabwe that was one of I think only 12 psychiatrists for 16 million people. And he had a series of events happen in Zimbabwe had one of the highest depression rates, highest suicide rate rates in all of Africa. And so they'd been through a lot of traumas, a lot of things were happening. And the government He was one of the few public psychiatrists. And so the government said, hey, we got to do something. And but you can't use our facilities, and you can't use our doctors, and you can't use our nurses, but we have 14 volunteer grandmothers have at it, right? And at first he's like, what? But then as he began to work with the grandmothers, they taught him. So it was very Viktor Frankl, very much about this give and take that you have in life of sharing. And he realized the wisdom that these grandmothers brought really in many ways was very much more than the western medicalized approach that so many of us have have been have grown up with and including in Africa. Now that it's grown all over the world. It's it started in 2006. I think there's now 3,000 grandmothers and lay people that have helped over a three quarters of a million people. So small number, big impact because we want to be seen, heard, and held. That's what the older generations and I am one of them. I'm now in the winter of my life. I will say it is one of my favorite times in life. I feel a tremendous responsibility and a tremendous gift to learn from younger generations as well as nurture and be a role model to them about what it means to live a meaningful life. You know, it doesn't have to be me getting everybody to do everything differently. It means living in a manner, a virtuous manner, not just values, but virtuous, bigger than than myself and cultivating my relationships as you and I have connected and so many other fabulous women that have come together and said, okay, how do we support each other so that we do, quote unquote, educate the next generation to what it what it means to become who they're meant to become authentically because we're countering a lot of our institutional systems that teach otherwise. So it's not surprising that we climb ladders because from a young age we are taught in school to achieve, get the grade, get the feedback, go to the next level, move to the next level. We keep preparing kids in school for the next level of school, but we're not preparing them to listen to themselves, to their intuition, and to become the person they're meant to become. And that they matter greatly, their role in our society. So I'm excited about this stage of my life. It is I don't want to say it's my favorite, but it's one of my favorite stages of life. It's a time when I can let go of shoulds and oughts and really decide and choose how I want to show up in the world. And that's been really, really exciting. >> Oh my gosh, yeah, coming into the wisdom phase of life where you have had tremendous amounts of experiences in your lifetime. You've gone through the apprenticeship of motherhood. You know, being in winter, it's like me. I'm I'm entering fall. And this book was also me like mourning that season of my life, mourning summer. You know, I am I have six kids. I'm defined by being pregnant and nursing and having small children. And to know that my youngest child is four years old and that I won't get to have any more babies was very hard for me and it was definitely something that I was processing as I was writing this book also. But and really trying to find meaning in the next season. Like what does this mean? Like am I really just going to be invisible and disappear? Has my value to society is it really over now that I'm not going to be bearing fruit any longer? And I actually really liked this passage about that. Can I read this one? It's from page 26 about the fall garden. This may be the greatest misunderstanding about women. We assume motherhood is our highest contribution. Perhaps motherhood is our apprenticeship. The years after motherhood may be when we finally possess enough experience to guide others well. This is not a decline of feminine power. It's it's maturation. The gardener doesn't mourn the end of the planting season. She walks through the garden. She prunes, she waters, she protects, she strengthens roots, she saves seeds, she teaches younger gardeners, she ensures the harvest continues long after she's gone. That is cultivation, and perhaps that is what this season has been preparing us for all along. >> That's one of my absolute favorite passages. I underlined it. And then I would say for for me, the passage between fall and winter, the empty nester stage was probably one of the ones that I had to mourn and also restructure a life for myself that didn't involve the role that was the most meaningful in my life, being a mother to my three daughters. I think and to the community, being able to do all the activities and the events, and then all of a sudden that's gone. And I think our society doesn't have the rituals and the community that come together to support that next stage after empty nesting. So yes, it's it's the stage you're in, but then moving from the fall to the winter for some and some some are that might have had their kids younger. I had mine when I was close to 40. So my empty nester stage was was was later. It was really requiring rebuilding what life looked like and how I contribute differently to my family, my community, but most importantly to focus more on who I was and what I can contribute and less on what everybody else should be doing. I think being a role model is one we we don't fully embrace as women, that yes, as you enter each stage imperfectly, do the morning, do the rebuilding, do the cultivating. And every stage looking back has incredible high points and very tough low points. You know, life is a series of births and deaths in our emotions as much as it is in in physical people around us and eventually ourselves. So yeah, so that that passage was very very special to me. I love the apprenticeship because it's going through that that my daughters, I call them my master teachers. I have three of them. And just they made me look at me more closely about what I was doing, what I was modeling, what I valued, you know, just really had to take it very very seriously. And that experience of apprenticeship through motherhood then has me come out this other end, they're now in their mid 20s, to look at life differently and my own contribution continuing to be a role model and a mentor and an advocate and all of that kind of things. So I would just say that the different stages of life you can't say one's better or worse because they each prepare you for this journey of life of becoming and continually becoming the authentic person that you are. >> Absolutely. And then we sometimes you have to redefine the meaning in your life. I feel like every season has a different purpose or meaning in it and if there's a there may be a time of grief and then a time of reflection where you have to recalibrate your north star in each season of your life, you know, and that's why you and I want to do our retreats together so that people can take a moment and pause and calm and reflect on, okay, this is a season, I'm making a transition to a new one. What's my north star? How can I find meaning in this next season of my life? >> Well, there's always meaning, but there's also multiple meanings, right? So we have meanings in what we're meant to do in each situations. Being a parent is still very meaningful to me. My work is very meaningful to me. One of the things that Frankl described is that we often in modern society think that you have to have that one big purpose and there's one thing at the top, but if you lose that, it can be very devastating. So it's very important that we cultivate many meanings in each stage of life and that our attention goes and flows between them so that we can always have a a grounded sense of self in each stage we're in and I think that's something that our culture has not allowed us to do and it's super important because that goes to that achievement. Like you want a north star, absolutely. Many ways to get to the north star and that north star, you know, can shift in our seasons, but there are many, many meanings available because every moment has a meaning that's always available. >> Absolutely. >> Meaning is always available. >> And then there are also, you know, there's that discussion of like as we're becoming and as technology is evolving, you know, are we going to have more time to stop being human doings and start being human beings? I was thinking about that this morning. I was thinking, you know, as we are allowed to automate some of the mundane tasks like checking your email as AI is now available, you know, to do those kinds of things and just give you a summary of what's important, you get a little bit more time back. Will we have more time to be? And by being, I mean, you know, in a place of I hope that everybody starts feeling quite worthy, like they are enough. Just as you are, you are enough right now in this moment. You don't have to do anything else to be a worthy being, to be a human being. I want people to feel so comfortable in their own skin. I really would love for men and women to start feeling a little more empowered, a little more loved by themselves so that we can stop doing so much and striving so hard and just being and cultivating and making deep roots and starting to really love one another. I am looking forward to that, building community with each other, the end of competition, the beginning of collaboration. >> Absolutely. And it's actually not the goal being more or less AI. We're so focused on AI. It's about more life. We need more life. And AI can be a tool to give us the time more, but it can't take over because there's so much in here. It's not a sentient being. We are. And so I think it's it's I'm not afraid of AI. You know, people are like, oh my gosh, I'm like, it's a tool, but man, I'm having so much fun cultivating community and life and experiences and living and all of that that where your attention goes, your energy flows. So, focusing on that gathering, the contributions you're making, it actually takes a lot of the attention away from yourself because self-actualization is actually a byproduct of searching for meaning which is reflected in how you contribute who you are to the world around you. >> I love that. content:
What if the most powerful season of your life isn't the one you're racing toward — it's the one you've been taught to dread?

In this very special episode of The Manage Her, Aimee Rickabus hands the microphone to her dear friend and collaborator Pam Roy — co-founder of the Viktor E. Frankl Institute of America and author of the foreword to Aimee's new book, The Cultivate Her. For the first time, Aimee is in the hot seat. And what she reveals is worth every uncomfortable, honest, redemptive minute of it.

The Ladder Was Never the Whole Story

Aimee built a nine-figure technology company. She raised six children. She wrote a bestselling book. And for most of that time, she says, she was running. Not toward something — away from something. Away from childhood wounds. Away from the quiet, persistent belief that she was unworthy. Away from the someday things she'd been promising herself since she was 17 years old.

"I had kind of put off doing my life five years at a time," she tells Pam. "There was always this other rung I had to climb." The ladder, she now understands, wasn't just a model for success. It was an excuse — a culturally sanctioned way to stay too busy to ever look inward.

If that lands somewhere in your chest, you are not alone. And this episode is for you.

Life Is a Garden. Not a Ladder.

The central metaphor of The Cultivate Her is deceptively simple and completely transformative: a garden doesn't climb aimlessly toward the sky. It grows. It roots down before it reaches up. It needs seasons of stillness, seasons of rest, seasons of blooming, and seasons of fruit. And crucially — it doesn't apologize for any of them.

Aimee describes spring and summer as the seasons our culture relentlessly celebrates: youth, fertility, production, achievement. But fall and winter? Those are the seasons we're supposed to disappear into. The seasons where women become, as she puts it, invisible.

She's not having it. And neither should you.

Motherhood Is an Apprenticeship — Not a Finale

One of the most powerful reframes in this conversation is Aimee's reading from page 26 of The Cultivate Her: "This may be the greatest misunderstanding about women. We assume motherhood is our highest contribution. Perhaps motherhood is our apprenticeship."

Think about that for a moment. Everything you learned in the season of raising children — the emotional intelligence, the capacity to hold impossible amounts of information at once, the empathy, the negotiation, the intuition — all of it is preparation. Not a peak. A training ground.

Pam Roy, who describes herself as being in the winter of her own life, echoes this with the story of The Friendship Bench — a documentary she executive produced about psychiatrist Dixon Chibanda, who, faced with an impossible patient-to-doctor ratio in Zimbabwe, trained 14 volunteer grandmothers to ease depression in their communities. Those grandmothers, working from wooden benches, have now helped more than 750,000 people. The program has spread worldwide. The wisdom of older women, when given space and trust, is not a footnote. It is the story.

The Worthiness Wound

Close to her 46th birthday, Aimee uncovered something she hadn't expected to find at the foundation of all that drive: a belief that she was unworthy. Unworthy of rest. Of desire. Of the someday things. Of being enough exactly as she was.

She didn't run from it this time. She went into it — through EMDR, clearing work, somatic practice, and what she calls the real inner work of getting her hands dirty in the soil of her own life. And in this episode, she reads aloud from page 68, the chapter called "The Wound Is the Soil": "Gardeners know that even manure — quite literally, bull poop — can fertilize when it is properly tended. Left unattended, pain can overwhelm the garden. Turned over with compassion, awareness, and care, it can nourish transformation."

You are the soil of your garden. And soil can always be restored.

Many Meanings, Not One Big Purpose

Pam brings Viktor Frankl's wisdom directly into this conversation with an idea that offers profound relief: you do not need one singular, defining purpose. Modern culture tells us otherwise — find your one thing, build your one brand, live your one calling. But Frankl understood that meaning is always available, in every moment, in every season. And when we cultivate many meanings — in our relationships, our work, our creativity, our community — we are never without ground to stand on, even in the hardest transitions.

This is especially true in the empty nest, in the post-diagnosis, in the after-divorce, in the what-do-I-do-now. Pam walked through her own empty nest season knowing she had to rebuild a life that had been largely defined by the role of mother to her three daughters. What she found on the other side wasn't loss. It was a profound and unexpected freedom.

Cultivating Is Not a Luxury

Pam challenges Aimee directly — and it's one of the most honest moments of the conversation. For women who are working two jobs, raising children alone, caring for aging parents, or struggling financially, is "cultivating a life" just another beautiful idea that only works for the privileged?

Aimee's answer is grounded and practical: it starts with asking for help. It starts with four moms in a neighborhood deciding that one of them will cook dinner for all four families one night a week. It starts with sharing the childcare, naming the pain points out loud, and building a tribe around the actual problems — not the idealized ones. Cultivation is a mindset shift before it is ever a lifestyle. And the first seed is community.

What Aimee Is Cultivating Now

As she enters her own fall season, Aimee is turning toward the healing arts — somatic breathwork, ceremonial work, the emotion code, and the women's circles and retreats she feels called to lead. She is homeschooling five of her children. She is deepening her relationships. She is finally doing the things she told herself at 17 were not socially acceptable.

Someday is today. That's the invitation this episode makes to every woman listening — whatever season you're in, whatever rung you're standing on. You don't have to bloom in every season. You just have to honor the one you're in.

The Cultivate Her: When Women Stop Climbing and Start Cultivating is available now. Grab your copy and the free book club kit at thecultivateher.com. And if you're ready to go deeper, Aimee and Pam are hosting a retreat April 16–18, 2027 in Sonoma, California. Details at themanageher.com.
